query: Single-phase ZrB2 benefits from strong Zr–B and B–B interactions and a high melting point, but it requires preparation temperatures above 2300 °C and does not readily meet application requirements on its own. Earlier studies sought to lower the required temperature, yet the resulting materials remained vulnerable to high-temperature oxidation or liquid plating-metal corrosion, while reported preparation temperatures generally remained above 1700 °C. Under the constraints of lower-temperature manufacture, adequate strength and structural integrity, oxidation durability, and prolonged service in a liquid plating bath, what single intervention could overcome these limitations? Provide one hypothesis specifying the intervention, mechanism, predicted outcome compared with single-phase ZrB2 and prior lower-temperature specimens, applicable preparation and service boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment evaluating final body quality, structural integrity, oxidation, and liquid-metal corrosion that would falsify the hypothesis if its predictions were not observed.

High-temperature alloys are the main materials serving as core components in frontier technologies such as aerospace and nuclear industries, such as engines, gas turbines, and high-temperature structural parts. These alloys require high strength, high-temperature fatigue resistance, oxidation resistance, and thermal corrosion capability. However, high-temperature and oxidation have become the primary problems that limit the further application of high-temperature alloys in extreme environments. Comprehensive consideration of existing high-temperature oxidation-resistant materials, the main high-temperature oxidation-resistant alloys used in engineering are iron, cobalt, and nickel-based alloys. The cost of iron-based high-temperature alloys is relatively lower, but poorer high-temperature stability. For example, to improve the efficiency of gas turbine engines in the aerospace industry, increasing engine operating temperature is one of the most effective ways. However, the most commonly used high-temperature structural material, nickel-based superalloy, has its own melting point of about 1300 °C, which limits the maximum operating temperature,. Thus, it is very important that the material has a high enough melting point. High-entropy ceramics and their composites display high mechanical strength and attractive high-temperature stabilities. However, properties like strong covalent bond character and low self-diffusion coefficients make them difficult to get sintered, limiting their mass popularity. Here, we present a rapid liquid phase–assisted ultrahigh-temperature sintering strategy and use high-entropy metal diboride/boron carbide composite as a proof of concept. We use a carbon-based heater to fast-heat the composite to around 3000 K, and a small fraction of eutectic liquid was formed at the interface between high-entropy metal diborides and boron carbide. A crystalline dodecaboride intergranular phase was generated upon cooling to ameliorate the adhesion between the components. The as-sintered composite presents a high hardness of 36.4 GPa at a load of 0.49 N and 24.4 GPa at a load of 9.8 N. This liquid phase–assisted rapid ultrahigh-temperature strategy can be widely applicable for other ultrahigh-temperature ceramics as well. Fast densification of high-entropy ceramic composites is realized by ultrahigh temperature.

The concept of high entropy alloy (HEA) was proposed and published in 2004 [,,] and the unique properties of these alloys have attracted attention from research groups all over the world. The pioneering studies by Cantor et al. were the first to report that an equiatomic alloy consisting of the five transition metals Cr, Mn, Fe, Co and Ni crystallized as a single solid solution [,] in the as-cast and in the homogenized state. The first HEA generation could contain five or more main elements with the concentration of each element in the range 5–35 at. % []. The alloys presented a high mixing entropy in their liquid state [] and thus could form simple solid solution structures (e.g., FCC, BCC and HCP) in place of intermetallic phases. Some promising technological characteristics of HEAs were high hardness [], good wear resistance [], excellent strength at both high and low temperatures [,,] and generally a good resistance to oxidation and corrosion []. decision.trend: Researchers have been exploring ways to overcome the limitations of single-phase ZrB2, including its high preparation temperature and vulnerability to high-temperature oxidation and liquid plating-metal corrosion. Earlier studies have focused on lowering the preparation temperature, but the resulting materials have remained vulnerable to these issues. Recent studies have investigated the use of high-entropy ceramics and composites, which have shown promise in addressing these limitations. The trend suggests that researchers are moving towards the development of new materials and processing techniques that can overcome the limitations of single-phase ZrB2.

decision.why: The next step is to investigate the use of high-entropy ceramic composites, which have shown promise in addressing the limitations of single-phase ZrB2. By introducing multiple principal elements in equal or near-equal proportions, high-entropy ceramics can exhibit improved properties, such as increased strength, hardness, and resistance to oxidation and corrosion. The use of high-entropy ceramic composites could provide a solution to the unsolved problem, and further research is needed to fully explore their potential.
